segments.title: The gap that had to fill
sections: The Gap That Had To Fill

cues.text: You know the morning. The open prints a hundred points above the prior day's high, the highest price traded in the prior session.
Gaps fill, you have heard it a hundred times. So at 9:31 a.m. you sell the open, with a stop, the resting order that takes you out, above the first bar.
At 9:36 the stop goes. At 9:44 you sell again, and that stop goes too.
At 12:40 p.m. price trades all the way down to the prior close without you. Early is a polite word for the stop going first.
You were not early. You had a target and no trade: no level, a price marked before the session, under the entry; no event that said now; and not even the right target.
This module gives the gap a definition one price can answer, a target that is a level, and an entry that needs a level and a trigger, the price event that says now.
Now, what counts as a gap.
A gap is an open outside the prior day's range. The open is the first trade of regular trading hours, 9:30 a.m. Eastern. Above the prior-day high is a gap up. Below the prior-day low is a gap down.
The course writes those two prices as PD High and PD Low, and you mark them before the session.
Take a prior range of 21,520 to 21,690, and a prior close of 21,671. An open at 21,742 is above 21,690. A gap up.
An open at 21,505 is below 21,520. A gap down.
An open at 21,682 is above the prior close but inside the range. Not a gap.
Many charting tools measure from the close and count it as one. That is a different event, and none of their numbers are used here.
An open at 21,640, inside the range after an overnight high of 21,760, is not a gap either. The overnight built the on-high and nothing more.
The rule: a gap is answered once, at the 9:30 print, from two prices written before the session.
Getting it wrong is calling the 21,682 open a gap and aiming at the prior close. You are borrowing a story that belongs to a different event.
The fix: on your pre-market sheet, write: gap if the open is above the PD High or below the PD Low, no gap between. At 9:30 write one word beside it: up, down or no.

segments.title: Gap Fill aims at the range edge
sections: Gap Fill Aims At The PD Range Edge

cues.text: Gap Fill is the gap setup that aims back at the prior day's range.
After a gap up it aims at the PD High. After a gap down, the PD Low. Never the prior close.
On a composite chart, invented prices: the open prints 21,792, above a PD High of 21,690. The pd-high zone, the band of prices around that level, runs 21,684 to 21,690.
Price arrives from above, so the edge it reaches first is 21,690. That is the target, 102 points below the open.
The prior close, 21,671, sits 19 points further down, inside the prior range. It is not on your level list, and it is not the target.
After a gap down the picture flips. The target is the PD Low, at the edge price reaches first from below.
A target is a level a trade aims at, written before entry. It is never a reason to enter, and never moved once the trade is on.
The planned scale still applies: half off at 2R, the runner to the level. R is the amount you risked on the trade.
Now, the numbers behind the rule. They come from TradingStats' NQ session-open data.
A touch means price traded at the line at any point from the 9:30 open to the 4 p.m. close.
On 811 sessions that opened above the prior range, price touched the prior high on 64.1 percent, and the prior close on 46.7 percent. TradingStats, n equals 811.
On 473 sessions that opened below the range, price touched the prior low on 67.0 percent, and the prior close on 45.9 percent. TradingStats, n equals 473.
The range edge was reached more often than the close. That is all. Not which way price went first, not when, not how far it ran against an entry.
The touch rate counts the visit. It never counts what you paid to wait.
The rule: after a gap up the target is the PD High; after a gap down, the PD Low. Never the prior close.
Getting it wrong is a target slot that says gap fill, or the prior close. You are trading a saying, and the saying picks the further, less-visited price.
The fix: the target slot takes one of two slugs, the short names you log a level under: pd-high or pd-low, with its price.
Any other word there, and the branch, that if-then line of the plan, is struck through before 9:25.

segments.title: The entry needs a level and a trigger
sections: The Entry Needs A Level And A Trigger

cues.text: Gap Fill gives you a target and a context, not an entry. The target says where, not where from, or when.
Same morning: the open prints 21,792, above a PD High of 21,690.
The open is not a location. It is where the first trade printed, so nothing sits behind a stop above it. It fails the stop-structure test from Module 6.
Now, where a trade can come from.
Two kinds of zone sit between the open and the target.
One: a zone the gap left in the way, such as the on-low, the overnight session's low, sitting above the prior-day high.
Two: an in-session level once formed, such as the opening range low after its window closes. The examples here use 9:30 to 9:45.
Now, the read and the trigger. At the zone, the read is the setup's own, judged on a closed bar.
Acceptance, Module 10: a 5-minute close beyond the zone within 15 minutes of the first touch. Or a failed breakdown and reclaim, Module 11.
Then a trigger, such as Pause N Go: a short pause inside the zone, then a close through its far edge, the side of the zone away from where price arrived.
Module 13 defines each one. Check the geometry at the trigger: the trade must clear 2 to 1, the target at least twice as far as the stop, which sits behind the far edge.
A zone too close to the target is no trade, however clean the trigger.
The journal records the ordinary setup, trend continuation or range rejection. The gap goes in the tags as context.
The rule: a branch on a gap morning names a zone between the open and the target, a read on a closed bar, and a trigger that fires in that zone.
No zone between the open and the target, no branch: the gap goes in the nothing case, the plan's no-trade line. A target with no zone under it is a wish with a price on it.
Getting it wrong is a sell at the open, with the stop above the first bar. The target is doing the job of the location.
The journal reads mid-range, no trigger: No Setup, the tag for a trade that had neither.
The fix: the open never goes on your level list, and no order is armed until a near-edge alert, set on the side of a zone price arrives at, fires.

segments.title: Gap N Go and your register
sections: Gap N Go Goes In Your Register, Not Your Plan

cues.text: Gap N Go is the idea that after a gap, price keeps travelling away from the prior day's range.
Traders talk about it every gap morning, and it is a fair idea to have. This course publishes no read, no trigger and no entry for it.
It sits in your parking lot, the list of ideas you have not tested. It leaves only as a locked, dated entry in your own register, the numbered page per idea that Modules 22 and 23 teach.
Now, the register entry. It has every slot a plan branch has, filled in before you open a single chart of past gap days.
One: the condition. The gap, exactly as this module defines it.
Two: location and read. A zone from your list, and what price must do there on a closed bar.
Three: trigger and window. One named trigger, and the clock times it may fire in.
Four: stop and target. The stop behind the far edge, the target a level.
Five: costs and the null. Commission and slippage per trade, and the baseline of shuffled data it has to beat.
Six: the locked date, written before any data was opened.
Module 22 carries the rest. Any setting you sweep, trying a range of values, is swept on a training window only, a slice of the data kept apart for that.
A filter that skips some sessions makes it a new entry. Sim trades, as in simulated, are counted apart from live ones.
The rule: Gap N Go stays in your parking lot until it is a locked, dated register entry. Until then, a gap morning with no triggered branch is the nothing case: no trade.
Getting it wrong is gap-and-go trades taken on mornings that looked strong, each with a slightly different entry and hold rule, chosen as the session went.
Strong-looking is not a condition. It is a mood with a chart. The definition moves with the outcome, so no count can form, and every result gets explained afterwards.
The fix: write the paragraph and date it before you open any data. Change one word later and it is a new entry number. The old entry stays as it was.

segments.title: The story, and one morning played two ways
sections: Worked Case: One Gap-Up Morning, Traded And Not

cues.text: "It has to fill." "It's going." Both arrive in the first minute, before a bar has closed. Both are forecasts. Neither is a level.
The bigger the gap, the louder the story. 64.1 percent, n equals 811, TradingStats, sounds like a promise. It is not. It counts sessions, including ones where your stop went first.
A gap feels like information about direction. It is information about where the open sat. Size comes from the grade, A-plus down to C, never from conviction, the Module 9 count.
The rule: the gap adds a target to the plan. It never adds a direction.
Getting it wrong is a second sell a minute after the first stop, with no new trigger, because it still has to fill.
The belief is doing the trigger's job. The gap has been saying that all morning. It has not placed an order yet.
The fix: a re-entry is the same setup plus a fresh trigger, its price condition written in the trade note first: one-minute close below 21,748.50. No line, no order.
The 2R kill switch from Module 2, the day's limit at twice one trade's risk, is the only cap.
Now, one gap-up morning, planned, then played two ways. A hypothetical illustration, not a trade record: a composite MNQ morning, invented prices.
The gap line: above 21,690 or below 21,520.
One branch: if price accepts below the on-low zone, 21,748 to 21,756, and Pause N Go fires on the first pullback into it, target pd-high, 21,690.
Invalidation is written first: a 5-minute close back above 21,756.
The open prints 21,792: gap line up, branch live. At 10:05 a 5-minute bar closes at 21,739, below the zone: acceptance. The branch waits for the pullback.
Morning one. Price comes back into the zone from below, holds two bars with no close above 21,756, then closes below the pause low.
Pause N Go fires. The stop sits two points behind the far edge, and the target clears 2 to 1.
Morning two. Same plan, same levels, same acceptance. Price never comes back. No pullback, no pause, no trigger.
By 10:41 the chart looks obvious. A sell there has nothing behind its stop, or fails 2 to 1.
The plan said where and when. One morning offered the when. The other did not: a branch that never triggered.
The target was reached both mornings. Only one had a trade in it.

check.q: What does a gap add to your plan?
check.why: The gap adds a target, never a direction. The size of the gap changes only the distance to the target.

check.q: Why is "64.1 percent touched" (TradingStats, n=811) not a promise?
options: It counts sessions, including ones where your stop went first
The sample is too small to read
check.why: A touch counts the visit. It does not count order of events, your entry, or whether the stop went first.

check.q: Your first sell on a gap morning stopped out. A minute later you want to sell again because it still has to fill. What do you need first?
options: Nothing, the setup is the same
A fresh trigger, with its price condition written in the trade note
check.why: A re-entry is the same setup plus a fresh trigger, written before the order. No line, no order.

check.q: On both mornings price accepts below the on-low zone. On morning two it never comes back. What is the result?
options: A late sell at a better price
No pause, no trigger, no trade
check.why: Without a pullback into the zone there is no pause and no trigger, so the branch never triggers and nothing is placed.

segments.title: Score it, then the assignment
sections: Is Your Gap Morning A Plan?

cues.text: Take your last five gap mornings, traded or not. Score each on seven lines, a point for every line that is true.
One: the gap line was written before 9:25 with both prices, and answered at 9:30 with one word.
Two: the target slot named pd-high or pd-low with its price.
Three: the branch named a zone between the open and the target.
Four: any entry came on a trigger that fired in that zone, not on the open or the first bar.
Five: the 2 to 1 check was done at the trigger.
Six: no trade in the gap's direction unless it matched a locked register entry.
Seven: every second entry had its own fresh trigger, written first.
Now, reading it. Lines three and four override the score. A trade that missed either was No Setup, however the rest scored.
If two or more of your five mornings missed line three or four, fix those first: no order until a near-edge alert on a named zone has fired.
Otherwise seven of seven is a gap plan. Six of seven plus a good feeling is a story. If two or more mornings scored under seven, fix the line you missed most.
Getting it wrong is scoring from memory. Memory keeps the morning that worked. The sheet and the journal keep all five, and they are the only place a score comes from.
The assignment. Before your next open, write the gap line on your sheet with both PD prices.
Under it, one line: gap up, target pd-high, and the price. Gap down, target pd-low, and the price. Two lines. That is the whole assignment.
In one line: a gap adds a target, pd-high or pd-low, and nothing else. The trade still needs a zone, a read and a trigger.
Where it goes next. Module 13, Triggers, teaches each price event a gap-morning trade can use. Module 14, Trade Construction, turns a triggered branch into an order.
Module 15 writes a gap branch into the plan, and the gap line is a field on the Module 16 sheet. The journal in Module 18 tags the gap as context.
Gap N Go goes through Module 22, How To Test An Edge, and Module 24, How Ideas Fail A Test.

check.q: A trade on a gap morning entered on the first bar, with the other six lines true. It is…
options: No Setup, because line four was missed
check.why: Lines three and four override the score. A trade that missed either one was No Setup, however the rest scored.

check.q: Two of your five gap mornings missed line three or four. What do you fix first?
options: Zones and triggers: no order until a near-edge alert has fired on a named zone
check.why: Fix lines three and four first: no order is armed on a gap morning until a near-edge alert on a named zone has fired.

check.q: What is the assignment?
options: Two lines on your sheet: the gap line with both PD prices, and a target line for each direction
Draw every prior close on the chart
check.why: Write the gap line with both PD prices, and under it the gap-up and gap-down target lines.

check.q: You score your last five gap mornings from memory. What does that reveal?
options: The morning you remember, not the five you traded
check.why: Memory keeps the morning that worked. The sheet and the journal keep all five, and the score comes only from them.

questions.q: A gap, in this course, is…
options: An open above the prior close
An RTH open outside the prior day's range
A fair value gap in the candles
Any move of 100 points at the open
questions.why: Above the PD High or below the PD Low at the 9:30 print. Anything between is no gap.

questions.q: After a gap down, Gap Fill's target is…
questions.why: The PD Low, at the edge price reaches first from below. Never the prior close.

questions.q: TradingStats NQ data (n=473) shows price touched the prior session low on 67.0 percent of gap-down sessions. What does it tell you?
options: The range edge was reached in that share of sessions, nothing about order or entry
questions.why: A touch rate counts visits to a line in a window. It does not say which way price went first or when.

questions.q: What must a gap-morning branch name?
options: A zone between the open and the target, a read, and a trigger that fires in that zone
The open price and a target
questions.why: An ordinary setup aimed at the PD range edge, with its trigger.

questions.q: You want to trade Gap N Go. The first step is…
options: Write and date a register entry before opening any data
Add it to the plan as a branch
questions.why: It has to exist as a locked, dated register entry first. Only your own record can say anything about it.

questions.q: After a stop on the first sell, you want a second sell toward the PD High. What is required first?
options: A fresh trigger, with its price condition written in the trade note
Nothing, the target has not changed
questions.why: A re-entry is the same setup plus a fresh trigger. No line, no order.

questions.q: Price accepts below your on-low zone but never comes back to it. What do you have?
questions.why: No pullback, no pause, no trigger. The result is recorded as a branch that never triggered.
